newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shares slightly up, lower Wall St impacts.
newsitem.headline: German shares slightly up, lower Wall St impacts.

text.p: The German IBIS DAX index hovered around the key 2,850-point mark on Monday afternoon, but prospects of further record gains were stymied by a weaker opening on Wall Street and uncertainty about Volkswagen.
The IBIS DAX index was slightly higher at 2,851.98 points at 1553 GMT, up 3.14, off the dizzy heights reached during bourse trade, with floor trade closing at 2,858.60 points.

"I'm still bullish for where this market is going. There will have to be some consolidation but with pressure on interest rates still there, we haven't seen the top of this market yet," said one DAX trader.
"The dark horse is on the other side of the Atlantic. If that takes a correction, markets on this side are going to have to pay attention," said the trader.
The Dow Jones Industrial index was down 0.65 percent at 6,479.96 points early on, which did not help sentiment in Frankfurt.

The main focus of the day was still on carmaker Volkswagen AG, which was the day's big loser. Shares in VW were down 30.75 marks, or nearly five percent, at 588 marks, as speculation raged about what would happen in the battle between VW and GM.

Banks were also lower. Commerzbank AG was down 37 pfennigs at 37.35 marks, Deutsche Bank was down 52 pfennigs at 72.60 marks and Dresdner was down 26 pfennigs at 45.39 marks. "The banks have been hit by profit-taking -- they've had a fantastic run lately," said one trader.
"The features on the upside are the chemical stocks, with BASF and Hoechst higher. SAP also seems to be re-tracing some of the ground it lost," said a trader.
BASF was up 98 pfennigs at 57.85 marks, while Hoechst AG was up 35 pfennigs at 67.93 marks. Degussa was up 25 marks at 663 marks after an earlier upbeat outlook.

"There's things going on but all-in-all it's thin trade -- a quiet Monday, pretty much dominated by the strength of the chemicals and Volkswagen, and really looking for a lead from the bond market or the U.S," a trader said.
